paragraphs.text: Lesson 21, leadership. Judy is struggling with her leadership role in a project, and Kevin
gives her some suggestions. Listen to their conversation and mark these statements true
or false.
I thought this new project would be a piece of cake, but it's turning out to be a real
pain.
Sorry to hear that. What's making it such a headache?
The committee just can't seem to agree on anything. Everyone has different ideas about
what we should do. They're also stubborn, and I'm at my wits end.
Okay, what's the goal of your project? Film me in on the details, maybe I can help you out.
We're trying to improve the children's center at the library. Just basic stuff like organizing
and adding more shelves indoors, then renovating the playground outside.
Seems pretty simple, so what's the issue?
Basically, Felix wants to sort through the old books before we start adding more shelves.
He says the books are outdated. Then, Cecily insists that we need to return the shelves we
already bought and get new, safer ones instead. Everyone's keen on improving the playground,
but half the people say they have back problems, so they won't be able to help. And the ones
that can work on the playground are bickering about which materials we should use.
Nice, eh?
Laura and Ned want to do a pizza fundraiser to get more money for the project. They want
to expand the playground to include a skateboard area and a climbing wall. But Heidi thinks we
should use the extra money to improve the handicapped ramps on the playground, and maybe
even add a wheelchair lift near the entrance.
It sounds like your group is great at brainstorming, but if you can't come to a consensus, then
you'll just be spinning your wheels forever.
You nailed it. At every meeting we get so bogged down in discussion that nothing gets done.
I'm supposed to be the leader, but if I put my foot down to make the decisions, some people
are always going to be upset.
Well, you can't please everyone. But the group does have to agree in advance that whatever
decisions are made, everybody will uphold them. Do you have a voting process?
No, for some reason we haven't thought about voting on things. It's just been a lot of talking
and arguing for hours on end.
Voting is great because everyone can voice their ideas, but then the majority decides
on what the group does. And since everyone's vote is equal, nobody can accuse you of favoritism.
That's a good idea. Got any other tips for me?
Another one is to make a clear distinction between what needs to be done and what people
want to do. This will help keep the group focused.
I like that. But what should we do about all the extra plans? There are some good ones in
there, and I don't want people feeling like their ideas are always shot down.
There are a couple of different approaches you could take, like voting on the extras and having
the group pick the best one. Another way is to divide the project into phase one, doing
only what's essential to the goal, and then phase two, adding extra stuff later.
Hey, and I just thought of something else. The people who are suggesting the extra stuff,
I could empower them to head up those projects. That way it wouldn't dull beyond my shoulders.
Now you're catching on? Remember that leading a group of people is definitely a learning process.
Let me know how your next meeting goes. Speaking of which, I gotta get ready because it starts
in an hour. Thanks Kevin. You've given me a lot of food for thought.
Let's learn the vocabulary from this discussion about being a leader.
Judy thought the new project would be a piece of cake. A piece of cake means very easy.
But she says it's turning out to be a real pain, and Kevin asks what's making it such a headache.
Both of these expressions, a real pain, and a headache, are used to describe something that is very annoying.
Judy says the problem is that the committee just can't seem to agree on anything. They're also stubborn.
The word stubborn describes a person who is convinced that they are right and doesn't change their mind easily.
Judy says, I'm at my wit's end. This expression means at the limit of your mental resources,
desperate and without additional options. Kevin asks Judy to fill him in on the details,
and maybe he can help. To fill someone in on something means to give that person information that they are lacking.
Judy explains the project, which involves basic stuff like organizing and adding more shelves indoors,
then renovating the playground outside. To renovate means to repair and improve a building or structure.
However, one of the team members wants to sort through the old books before adding more shelves.
To sort through means to go through a collection and organize or classify the items.
This person says the books are outdated. Outdated means old-fashioned, not modern.
According to Judy, everyone's keen on improving the playground. Keen on means excited about.
However, some people are bickering about which materials to use. The word bickering means arguing, often over small,
insignificant things that are not really important in the big picture.
Judy elaborates further, saying that Laura and Ned want to do a pizza fundraiser.
A fundraiser is an event for getting monetary donations for a project or cause.
But Heidi thinks we should use the extra money to improve the handicapped ramps.
The word handicapped refers to people with disabilities, and ramps are inclined areas,
so Heidi wants to improve the inclined areas that people with wheelchairs can use instead of going up steps.
Kevin observes that the group is great at brainstorming.
The word brainstorming means creating many new ideas.
However, the group can't come to a consensus. The word consensus means agreement.
Kevin points out that you'll be doing nothing more than spinning your wheels.
The expression spinning your wheels means wasting time, staying in the same position,
and not making progress or advancing.
Judy replies, you nailed it.
You nailed it means you're exactly right.
She says, at every meeting we get so bogged down in discussion that nothing gets done.
Bogged down means stuck, slow, unable to make good progress.
Judy is supposed to be the leader, but she says if she puts her foot down and makes the decision,
some people are going to be upset.
To put your foot down means to take a firm position on something.
Kevin's first tip is that the group must agree in advance that whatever decisions are made,
everybody will uphold them. The word uphold means support.
He then suggests voting.
Judy says they haven't tried this.
It's just been a lot of talking and arguing for hours on end.
Hours on end means many consecutive hours.
Kevin says that voting is great because everyone can voice their ideas.
In this sentence, voice is being used as a verb meaning to express.
Everyone can express their ideas.
And because everyone's vote is equal, nobody can accuse the leader of favoritism.
Favoritism means giving some people unfair special preference.
Another of Kevin's suggestions is to keep the group focused on what needs to be done,
as opposed to what people want to do.
But Judy doesn't want to discard the extra plans completely.
She says, I don't want people feeling like their ideas are always shot down.
If an idea or proposal is shot down, it means it is criticized and then rejected.
So, Kevin proposes having the group vote on the extras and pick the best one.
Pick means to select, and another option is to divide the project into two phases.
Then, Judy comes up with her own idea, to empower the people who are suggesting the extra stuff to head up those projects.
The verb empower means to give someone power or authority.
And head up means lead or be responsible for.
So, Judy wants to give some people the power or authority to lead the extra projects.
That way, she says, it wouldn't all be on my shoulders.
On my shoulders means my responsibility.
Kevin replies, now you're catching on.
You're catching on means you're starting to understand.
And Kevin wants to know how the next meeting goes.
Judy then says, speaking of which, I gotta get ready.
We use the phrase, speaking of which, when something the other person just mentioned,
reminds us of something we want to say about that topic.
So, Kevin mentioned the next meeting, and Judy is reminded of the fact that she has a meeting very soon.
Judy thanks Kevin and says, you've given me a lot of food for thought.
Food for thought means things to think about and consider carefully.
That's all the vocabulary from today's conversation.
Go ahead and try the vocabulary quiz to put these expressions into practice,
and the speaking task to get some feedback on your spoken English.
